notes:
Task and constraints: Find the shortest contiguous subarray whose length equals the array's degree.
Idea: Count each value, record its first and last index, then minimize the span for values with maximum frequency.
Technique and why it applies: The degree is the largest frequency. A subarray containing every occurrence of a value must cover its first through last index, so that span is the shortest for that value.
Invariant: left and right store the earliest and latest indices of each value, and counts stores its frequency.
Edge cases: nums is assumed nonempty because max(counts.values()) is called. Repeated values are handled by the frequency map.
Complexity: The scans take O(n) expected time and O(u) space for u distinct values.

Task and constraints: Decide whether nums can be partitioned into k subsets with equal sums.
Idea: Backtrack over values, filling one subset to the target at a time while tracking used indices.
Technique and why it applies: A subset closes when curr reaches limit, after which recursion starts another. visited prevents reuse; duplicate-adjacent and empty/full-subset pruning attempt to reduce equivalent branches.
Invariant: visited marks values already assigned to earlier or current subsets, and curr is the current subset sum.
Edge cases: The total must divide evenly by k, there must be at least k numbers, and no number may exceed the target. nums is not sorted, so adjacent-duplicate pruning is less effective.
Complexity: Worst-case backtracking is exponential, up to O(k^n) assignments, with O(n) visited state and recursion depth.

Task and constraints: Partition all numbers into k equal-sum subsets.
Idea: Sort values descending and recursively assign each number to one of k bucket sums.
Technique and why it applies: A number is placed only when the bucket remains at or below target. If a placement fails, it is undone; the break after failing to fill an empty bucket avoids symmetric bucket permutations.
Invariant: subset_sums records the current sum of each bucket, and all processed values have been assigned exactly once.
Edge cases: The total must be divisible by k, and the largest value cannot exceed target. Sorting mutates nums and helps large values fail early.
Complexity: The backtracking search is exponential in n in the worst case, with O(n) recursion and O(k) bucket storage.

Task and constraints: Determine whether nums can be divided into k equal-sum subsets.
Idea: Memoize states by a bitmask of used elements and recursively choose an unused value that fits the current bucket remainder.
Technique and why it applies: todo tracks the sum still needed across all unfinished buckets. The expression (todo-1)%target+1 gives the remaining amount in the current bucket, and reaching the full used mask is success.
Invariant: lookup[used] records whether the subset of indices represented by used can be completed into valid target-sum buckets.
Edge cases: A non-divisible total or a number larger than target returns False. The method assumes positive numbers and target greater than zero.
Complexity: There are O(2^n) bitmask states and each may scan n values, giving O(n·2^n) time and O(2^n) memo space.

Task and constraints: Compute the skyline height after dropping squares in sequence, returning the maximum height after each drop.
Idea: Coordinate-compress square endpoints and use square-root decomposition arrays to query and update interval heights.
Technique and why it applies: query combines per-position heights with full-block maxima; each new square rests on the maximum height over its covered interval, then update raises the covered heights and block summaries.
Invariant: heights stores detailed local maxima, blocks stores full-block values, and blocks_read stores partial-block maxima used during range queries.
Edge cases: The coordinate list includes left and left+size-1, treating integer positions as inclusive. The code defines segment-tree classes too, but the active solution uses the block-decomposition helpers.
Complexity: With W distinct endpoints and block size about sqrt(W), each range query/update is roughly O(sqrt(W)); total is about O(n sqrt(W)) after sorting/compression, with O(W) space.

Task and constraints: Return the maximum skyline height after each square falls onto the previous squares.
Idea: For each square, find the highest overlapping earlier square, add the new side length, and propagate heights to later overlapping squares.
Technique and why it applies: An overlap means the later square must rest at least as high as the earlier square's top. heights[j] is updated with max(heights[j], heights[i]) when their horizontal intervals intersect.
Invariant: heights[i] is the height reached by square i after considering earlier overlapping squares, and result stores the running maximum.
Edge cases: The overlap test uses half-open intervals [left,right), so touching edges do not overlap. Despite unused segment-tree definitions, the active method is the nested-loop implementation.
Complexity: Every pair of squares may be compared, giving O(n²) time and O(n) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Compute the maximum skyline height after each falling square.
Idea: Coordinate-compress endpoints and maintain an ordered list of segment boundaries and heights.
Technique and why it applies: bisect locates the covered segment range; the square's base is the maximum existing height in that slice, and its top is base+side. The interval is replaced by the new boundary and height entries.
Invariant: pos stores sorted segment boundaries, heights stores the corresponding skyline segments, and maxH is the highest top seen so far.
Edge cases: The code assumes at least one valid square and uses half-open right boundaries. Replacing slices can shift many list elements.
Complexity: Binary searches are O(log n), but list slice replacement and max over slices can take O(n) per square, giving O(n²) worst-case time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Find target in a sorted array and return its index, or -1 if absent.
Idea: Apply iterative binary search over the current candidate interval.
Technique and why it applies: The midpoint comparison discards the half that cannot contain target, relying on sorted order.
Invariant: If target exists, its index remains within [left,right].
Edge cases: Empty arrays skip the loop and return -1. If duplicates existed, any matching index could be returned; the problem specifies distinct values.
Complexity: Each iteration halves the search range, giving O(log n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Search for target in a sorted array of distinct integers.
Idea: Repeatedly inspect the midpoint and narrow the search interval based on its value.
Technique and why it applies: Sorted order means values smaller than target lie to the right of the midpoint and larger values lie to the left.
Invariant: The remaining interval [left,right] contains target if it occurs in nums.
Edge cases: Empty input returns -1. The midpoint formula avoids adding left and right directly, which also avoids overflow in fixed-width integer languages.
Complexity: Binary search takes O(log n) time and O(1) extra space.

Task and constraints: Convert uppercase English letters in a string to lowercase.
Idea: Map each uppercase character to its lowercase code point and leave other characters unchanged.
Technique and why it applies: For ASCII letters, lowercase code points are 32 greater than uppercase ones, so the expression offsets ord(c) from 'A' to 'a'.
Invariant: Each output character is the lowercase version of its input character if it is in A–Z; otherwise it is unchanged.
Edge cases: Non-uppercase characters, including punctuation and digits, pass through unchanged. The method assumes the requested ASCII English-letter behavior.
Complexity: One pass creates the output, giving O(n) time and O(n) output space.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum total ASCII value of characters deleted from s1 and s2 to make the strings equal.
Idea: Use memoized recursion over prefixes, choosing matching characters together or deleting one of the two differing characters.
Technique and why it applies: Matching characters need no deletion. If characters differ, the cheaper option deletes s1[i] or s2[j], adding that character's ASCII code to the recursive cost.
Invariant: fun(i,j) is the minimum delete sum needed to make prefixes s1[:i+1] and s2[:j+1] equal.
Edge cases: Empty-prefix cases sum the ASCII values of the remaining prefix. Those base cases are not memoized and repeatedly compute sums, adding overhead.
Complexity: There are O(mn) memo states, but repeated prefix sums can raise the worst-case runtime toward O(mn(m+n)); memo space is O(mn).

Task and constraints: Minimize the sum of deleted character ASCII values required to make two strings equal.
Idea: Fill a two-dimensional DP table for prefixes of s1 and s2.
Technique and why it applies: Boundary cells accumulate the ASCII cost of deleting an entire prefix. Matching characters carry the diagonal cost forward; mismatches choose the cheaper deletion from either string.
Invariant: dp[i][j] is the minimum delete sum to make the first i characters of s1 and first j characters of s2 equal.
Edge cases: Empty strings are handled by the initialized first row and column. Matching characters do not need to be deleted.
Complexity: The table has O(mn) states with constant work each, so time and space are O(mn).

Task and constraints: Compute the minimum ASCII delete sum for two strings using reduced memory.
Idea: Use two rolling DP rows instead of retaining the full prefix table.
Technique and why it applies: Each state depends only on the previous s1 row, the previous column in the current row, and the diagonal. Matching characters use the diagonal; mismatches add the ASCII cost of deleting one character.
Invariant: dp[(i+1)%2][j] stores costs for the current s1 prefix, while dp[i%2][j] stores costs for the previous prefix.
Edge cases: The first row accounts for deleting prefixes of s2, and each new row initializes its first column by deleting the s1 prefix.
Complexity: Time is O(mn) and auxiliary DP space is O(n).

Task and constraints: Count contiguous subarrays whose product is strictly less than k.
Idea: Maintain a sliding window product and shrink from the left until the product is below k.
Technique and why it applies: With positive integers, extending the right endpoint multiplies the product; while it is too large, dividing out the leftmost value restores validity. Each valid window ending at fin contributes fin-ini+1 subarrays.
Invariant: After shrinking, p is the product of nums[ini:fin+1] and is less than k.
Edge cases: k<=1 returns zero because positive products cannot be less than it. The method assumes nums contains positive values; zero values would complicate integer division-based shrinking.
Complexity: Each index enters and leaves the window at most once, giving O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Maximize stock-trading profit when each completed sale incurs a transaction fee.
Idea: Memoize the best future profit by day and whether the next action is to buy or sell.
Technique and why it applies: In the buy state, choose between buying now and waiting. In the holding state, choose between selling now after the fee and continuing to hold.
Invariant: f(ind,buy) is the maximum profit achievable from day ind onward under the specified holding state.
Edge cases: Reaching day n returns zero. The recursive approach assumes prices is a valid nonempty sequence only insofar as the base case handles its length; an empty list returns zero.
Complexity: There are O(n) day/state pairs and constant transitions, so O(n) time and O(n) memo/recursion space.

Task and constraints: Maximize profit from stock transactions with a fixed fee charged on every sale.
Idea: Maintain best profit while not holding stock (cash) and while holding stock (hold).
Technique and why it applies: Each day's cash can remain unchanged or sell the held stock for price-fee; hold can remain unchanged or buy at today's price using available cash.
Invariant: cash is the best profit after the day without stock, and hold is the best profit after the day with stock.
Edge cases: The code initializes hold from prices[0], so it assumes prices is nonempty. The fee is deducted only on selling.
Complexity: One pass uses O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Determine whether the final character in a bit encoding is a one-bit character, given that the encoding ends with zero.
Idea: Scan backward from the bit before the final zero, toggling a boolean for each consecutive one until a zero appears.
Technique and why it applies: A run of ones immediately before the last zero determines how that zero is parsed: an even run leaves it as a one-bit character, while an odd run pairs it with a preceding one.
Invariant: ret records the parity of the consecutive ones encountered while scanning backward.
Edge cases: The problem guarantees the final bit is zero and the list is nonempty. A penultimate zero stops the scan and returns True.
Complexity: The backward scan is O(n) time and O(1) space.

Task and constraints: Check whether the last bit is a standalone one-bit character.
Idea: Count the parity of consecutive ones immediately before the final zero.
Technique and why it applies: Starting from the penultimate bit, each one toggles parity; the first zero ends the run. Even parity means the last zero begins a one-bit character, while odd parity means it belongs to a two-bit character.
Invariant: parity is the parity of the current suffix run of ones before the terminal zero.
Edge cases: The input is assumed to end with zero as guaranteed by the problem. A final preceding zero yields parity zero and True.
Complexity: One backward scan takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Find the maximum length of a common contiguous subarray of nums1 and nums2.
Idea: Use dynamic programming where a matching pair extends the common suffix ending at the previous pair of positions.
Technique and why it applies: If nums1[col] equals nums2[row], the common contiguous length is one plus the diagonal state; otherwise the state resets to zero.
Invariant: dp[row][col] is intended to be the common-suffix length ending at those two positions.
Edge cases: The extra row and column provide zero boundary values. At row zero, negative indexing reads the last row, which is still zero at that point because rows are processed in order; this is unusual but relies on initialization and iteration order.
Complexity: The nested loops take O(mn) time and the table uses O(mn) space.

Task and constraints: Find the kth smallest absolute difference among all pairs of array elements.
Idea: Enumerate every pair and maintain a max-heap of the k smallest distances seen so far.
Technique and why it applies: Distances are stored as negative values, making the heap root the largest distance currently retained. Whenever size exceeds k, that largest retained distance is removed.
Invariant: After processing each pair, the heap contains up to k smallest distances among all pairs seen so far.
Edge cases: k is assumed valid and there must be at least one pair. The original values need not be sorted because absolute difference is used.
Complexity: There are O(n²) pairs, each with O(log k) heap work, giving O(n² log k) time and O(k) heap space.
